adrs.title: Record architecture decisions
adrs.body:
# Record architecture decisions

## Context and Problem Statement

Ledgerly's design choices live in chat threads and pull-request comments. New contributors cannot tell which choices still hold, and old debates restart every quarter. How do we keep a durable, reviewable record of decisions?

## Considered Options

* Markdown ADRs in the repository (MADR 4)
* A wiki page per decision
* No formal record

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Markdown ADRs in the repository", because records are reviewed in the same pull requests as the code they shape and travel with every clone.

### Consequences

* Good, because decisions are versioned with the code.
* Bad, because someone has to keep statuses current when decisions change.

## More Information

Records live in `docs/adr/` and are managed with the `adr` plugin. See [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) for the template.

adrs.title: Use PostgreSQL as the primary datastore
adrs.body:
# Use PostgreSQL as the primary datastore

## Context and Problem Statement

The ledger needs transactional writes, foreign keys and reporting queries over a few million rows per tenant. Which database do we build on?

## Decision Drivers

* Strong consistency for double-entry postings
* Mature migration tooling
* Operations cost for a two-person team

## Considered Options

* PostgreSQL 16 on a managed host
* MySQL 8
* SQLite

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "PostgreSQL 16 on a managed host", because it gives us serializable transactions and the richest SQL for reports.

### Consequences

* Good, because `CHECK` constraints enforce balanced postings in the database.
* Bad, because every preview environment needs its own database instance.

## More Information

Recorded under the process in ADR-0001.

adrs.title: Expose a REST API with JSON envelopes
adrs.body:
# Expose a REST API with JSON envelopes

## Context and Problem Statement

The web app, the mobile app and two partner integrations read the same ledger data. They need one stable contract with predictable errors and pagination.

## Considered Options

* REST with JSON envelopes
* gRPC with a REST gateway
* GraphQL

| Option | Client effort | Caching | Tooling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| REST + envelopes | Low | HTTP caches work | OpenAPI |
| gRPC + gateway | Medium | Gateway only | Protobuf |
| GraphQL | Medium | Custom | Codegen |

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "REST with JSON envelopes", because every client already speaks HTTP and the envelope keeps errors uniform.

```json
{ "data": [{ "id": "pst_91" }], "next": "c2VxOjEwMjQ=", "error": null }
```

### Consequences

* Good, because partners can use plain `curl` to explore.
* Neutral, because pagination cursors are opaque keys from the primary store (ADR-0002).
* Bad, because over-fetching on the dashboard needs dedicated endpoints.

## More Information

The OpenAPI document is generated from route handlers on every build.

adrs.title: Authenticate with server-side session cookies
adrs.body:
# Authenticate with server-side session cookies

## Context and Problem Statement

The first release has a single web client on the same origin as the API. How should users sign in?

## Considered Options

* Server-side sessions in an `HttpOnly` cookie
* Self-issued JWTs in local storage

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Server-side sessions", because they are revocable and immune to token theft through XSS.

### Consequences

* Good, because logout is immediate.
* Bad, because the mobile app and partners cannot use cookies cleanly.

adrs.title: Run on SQLite with Litestream replication
adrs.body:
# Run on SQLite with Litestream replication

## Context and Problem Statement

Managed PostgreSQL costs more than the rest of our hosting combined, and per-preview databases slow every pull request. Most tenants are small. Can a single-node store carry us through the beta?

## Decision Drivers

* Hosting cost during the beta
* Preview environments in seconds
* Point-in-time recovery

## Considered Options

* SQLite in WAL mode with Litestream to object storage
* Keep managed PostgreSQL
* PostgreSQL in a container per node

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "SQLite with Litestream", because it removes the database bill and makes previews instant while keeping continuous backups.

### Consequences

* Good, because a preview is a file copy.
* Bad, because we are limited to **one writer node**.
* Bad, because reporting queries compete with postings for the same file.

### Confirmation

A weekly restore drill must finish inside the 15-minute RTO.

## More Information

### 2026-05-30

Restore drill from Litestream took 4 minutes for 2.1 GB; within the RTO. Write latency p99 rose to 38 ms under the month-end batch.

notes.text: Restore drill from Litestream took 4 minutes for 2.1 GB; within the RTO. Write latency p99 rose to 38 ms under the month-end batch.

adrs.title: Use OIDC with short-lived access tokens
adrs.body:
# Use OIDC with short-lived access tokens

## Context and Problem Statement

The mobile app and partner integrations cannot rely on same-origin cookies. We need one sign-in flow for every client of the API described in ADR-0003.

## Considered Options

* OIDC with a hosted identity provider, 10-minute access tokens and rotating refresh tokens
* Long-lived API keys per client
* Keep cookies and add a token bridge

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "OIDC with a hosted identity provider", because it serves browsers, mobile and machine clients with one standard.

### Consequences

* Good, because revocation is bounded by the 10-minute token lifetime.
* Bad, because the identity provider becomes a hard dependency for sign-in.

## More Information

### 2026-06-11

Refresh-token rotation shipped in mobile 2.4. Partner keys are migrated; the cookie session endpoint returns `410 Gone`.

notes.text: Refresh-token rotation shipped in mobile 2.4. Partner keys are migrated; the cookie session endpoint returns `410 Gone`.

adrs.title: Introduce a GraphQL gateway
adrs.body:
# Introduce a GraphQL gateway

## Context and Problem Statement

The dashboard makes nine REST calls on load. The mobile team asked for a GraphQL gateway in front of the REST API (ADR-0003).

## Considered Options

* GraphQL gateway over the REST endpoints
* Two aggregate REST endpoints for the dashboard

## Decision Outcome

Rejected. Two aggregate endpoints remove eight of the nine calls without a second API surface to secure, version and monitor.

### Consequences

* Good, because there is still one contract to document.
* Bad, because new screens may need new aggregate endpoints.

adrs.title: Generate exports with a nightly cron job
adrs.body:
# Generate exports with a nightly cron job

## Context and Problem Statement

Accountants download CSV and DATEV exports. Building them on request blocked the single writer for minutes.

## Considered Options

* Nightly cron that writes exports to object storage
* On-demand exports in a background worker

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Nightly cron", because it runs while traffic is lowest and needs no queue.

### Consequences

* Good, because postings are never blocked during the day.
* Bad, because exports are up to 24 hours old.

## More Information

### 2026-09-15

Deprecated. Exports now stream on demand from the read replica introduced in ADR-0009; the cron job is switched off.

notes.text: Deprecated. Exports now stream on demand from the read replica introduced in ADR-0009; the cron job is switched off.

adrs.title: Move back to managed PostgreSQL with read replicas
adrs.body:
# Move back to managed PostgreSQL with read replicas

## Context and Problem Statement

Three enterprise tenants joined after the beta. The single SQLite writer now saturates at month end, and reports slow down postings. The cost argument from ADR-0005 no longer holds at this volume.

## Decision Drivers

* Write throughput at month end
* Isolating reports from postings
* Recovery time under 15 minutes

## Considered Options

* Managed PostgreSQL 17 with one read replica
* Shard SQLite per tenant
* Stay on SQLite and queue writes

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Managed PostgreSQL 17 with one read replica", because it scales writes vertically and moves every report to the replica. It returns to the store chosen in ADR-0002 with a different topology.

### Consequences

* Good, because reports and exports no longer touch the primary.
* Good, because the schema from the PostgreSQL era still applies with two migrations.
* Bad, because previews need a database again; we use template databases to keep them under a minute.

### Confirmation

1. Month-end batch completes with p99 write latency below 20 ms.
2. Restore drill passes from the provider's point-in-time recovery.

## More Information

Migration runbook: `ops/runbooks/sqlite-to-postgres.md`.

### 2026-08-02

Cut-over finished in 11 minutes of read-only mode. Month-end p99 write latency is 9 ms.

notes.text: Cut-over finished in 11 minutes of read-only mode. Month-end p99 write latency is 9 ms.

adrs.title: Keep an append-only audit log of postings
adrs.body:
# Keep an append-only audit log of postings

## Context and Problem Statement

Auditors ask who changed a posting and when. Updates overwrite rows, so the answer depends on application logs that expire after 30 days.

## Decision Drivers

* Seven-year retention required by GoBD
* Tamper evidence
* No extra load on the primary (see ADR-0009)

## Considered Options

* Append-only `posting_events` table with hash chaining
* Logical replication into a separate audit store
* Trigger-based history tables

## Decision Outcome

Proposed option: "Append-only `posting_events` table with hash chaining", because it keeps the audit trail in the same transaction as the posting. The actor comes from the OIDC subject (ADR-0006).

### Consequences

* Good, because every change is attributable.
* Bad, because storage grows by roughly 40% per year.

## More Information

Open question: do we need to *redact* personal data inside events for erasure requests?

adrs.title: Adopt OpenTelemetry for request tracing
adrs.body:
# Adopt OpenTelemetry for request tracing

## Context and Problem Statement

Slow requests are hard to explain because API, worker and database logs share no request id.

## Considered Options

* OpenTelemetry SDK with an OTLP collector
* Vendor agent from our log provider

## Decision Outcome

Draft. Leaning towards OpenTelemetry to avoid lock-in.
